title: NYC Cannabis Dispensary Market — Where the Unit Economics Actually Work
text: Type: Analysis (operator decision memo) · Domain: Regulated cannabis market, NY Office of Cannabis Management (OCM) Method: Public OCM licensing data · Comparative submarket analysis · Scoring framework Status: Final report · Role: Analyst

title: NYC Cannabis Dispensary Market — Where the Unit Economics Actually Work
text:
Core question
Adult-use cannabis legalized in NY in 2023. The NYC dispensary market has been a fragmented, partially-illegal rollout — uneven license issuance, parallel unlicensed market, regulatory uncertainty, sharp variance across submarkets.
The decision this memo answers:

Out of the operating environments available in NYC, which submarkets and operator strategies have unit economics that survive the first 3–5 years of regulatory tightening — and which look attractive in the aggregate data but are bait traps for new entrants?

title: NYC Cannabis Dispensary Market — Where the Unit Economics Actually Work
text:
Why this matters
The first wave of post-CAURD operators has produced wildly different outcomes depending on location, license type, and operational discipline. Generic industry forecasts treat the NYC dispensary market as one number; the reality is high variance across submarkets driven by zoning, enforcement pressure, foot traffic, demographic mix, and competitive density (both licensed and unlicensed).
Picking the right submarket is the single biggest predictor of whether a dispensary survives. A scoring framework that holds up under operational scrutiny — not just an industry-overview deck — is what an actual operator needs.

title: NYC Cannabis Dispensary Market — Where the Unit Economics Actually Work
text:
Method
Three-stage operator analysis. Deliverables A, B, and C correspond to the three stages.

Stage 1 — Framework definition (Deliverable A: full report)
Defined the decision criteria explicitly:

Unit economics — revenue per sqft, expected gross margin, payback period, working capital intensity
Competitive density — licensed dispensary count + unlicensed retailer footprint within a measurable radius
Regulatory exposure — zoning, enforcement track record by precinct, license-type constraints
Operator-side requirements — capex, license type implications, location lock-in
Demographic and foot-traffic signal — density, daytime vs. residential, retail corridor character

Built a scoring rubric that could be applied consistently across candidate locations and operator strategies — the same lens applied uniformly is what lets the analysis hold up under interrogation.


Stage 2 — Market analysis

Mapped the licensed and unlicensed retailer footprint across NYC at the time of analysis
Profiled vertical segments: retail dispensary, delivery, processing/manufacturing, cultivation, ancillary services to licensed operators
Identified the structural dynamics compressing margins fastest (license-issuance acceleration, unlicensed enforcement variance, supply-side capex)



Stage 3 — Scoring and shortlist (Deliverables B and C)

Applied the scoring model from Stage 1 to candidate locations and strategies
Produced a ranked shortlist with a unit-economics view per option
Flagged which strategies looked attractive in aggregate market data but were vulnerable to the specific failure modes surfaced in Stage 2

title: NYC Cannabis Dispensary Market — Where the Unit Economics Actually Work
text:
Key findings

Licensed retail margins compress fast as license issuance accelerates. First-mover advantage is real but short; the early-licensee economics are not replicable for entrants who arrive 18 months later. Modeling the early-cohort margin as a forecast for entrants in 2026 is the most common mistake in the industry decks.
Delivery is structurally worse than the marketing suggests. Last-mile compliance costs, narrow basket sizes, and platform fees crush unit economics for any operator without an existing retail anchor. Pure-play delivery operators in the analyzed dataset consistently underperformed retail on a contribution-margin basis.
Processing and manufacturing show the most defensible margins. Capex is meaningful but workflow IP and B2B relationships create real moat. Several strongest operators in NYC at the time of analysis were vertically integrated upstream — that’s where the spread between the public narrative and the actual P&L is widest.
Ancillary services to licensed operators (compliance software, lab testing, security) are the under-discussed opportunity. Lower regulatory exposure, transferable across states, and the buyer is a regulated operator with a real procurement budget and no incumbent vendor of substance.
The unlicensed market is the binding constraint on every licensed submarket. Until enforcement materially changes storefront density, licensed retail competes on a tilted field — and the variance is per-block, not aggregate. The single biggest predictor of licensed-retail revenue at the time of analysis was the count of unlicensed storefronts within a ten-block radius.

title: NYC Cannabis Dispensary Market — Where the Unit Economics Actually Work
text:
Recommendation
For a new operator in 2026:

Don’t enter retail unless you have a unique cost-of-capital or location advantage that isn’t already priced into early-licensee bids
Two strongest entry points: upstream processing/manufacturing (defensible margins, real moat) or ancillary services to licensed operators (lower regulatory exposure, multi-state portability)
Delivery is a value trap absent existing retail anchors
The asymmetric upside is in compliance and operations software for licensed operators — a small, growing buyer base with a real procurement budget and no incumbent solution

The detailed location- and strategy-level shortlist sits in Deliverable C.

title: NYC Cannabis Dispensary Market — Where the Unit Economics Actually Work
text:
What I’d investigate next

Concrete bottom-up unit economics on the top three vertically-integrated operators (most public data is operator-friendly press, not financials)
Actual basket size and CAC trajectory for delivery operators after the 2024–25 enforcement actions (the enforcement step-change should materially shift delivery economics — needs a follow-up scan)
Whether 2025–26 MSO capital changes the licensed-retail calculus — large multi-state operators entering NY at scale could re-rate the competitive density faster than the current trajectory implies

title: NYC Cannabis Dispensary Market — Where the Unit Economics Actually Work
text:

Stage 1 — Framework: Scoring criteria, decision rubric, regulatory map (8KB memo)
Stage 2 — Market analysis: Submarket dynamics, competitive density, regulatory exposure (18KB)
Deliverable A — Full report: Compiled 32-page memo
Deliverable B — Scoring model: Per-location and per-strategy scoring with weights
Deliverable C — Ranked shortlist: Top siting options + strategy recommendations

title: Application Assistant
text: Type: Product · Domain: Job-application workflow / candidate-role fit Stack: Python · Flask · Anthropic Claude API (Opus 4.8) · OpenAI (GPT-4.1 + transcription) · pdfplumber · python-docx · Docker · Render Status: Deployed web app (cover-letter-assistant.onrender.com) · Role: Sole builder

title: Application Assistant
text:
One-line summary
A Flask web app with three modes that share one principle: do the analytical work before writing. It tailors cover letters, rebuilds a resume against a specific JD, and prepares grounded “why this company / why this role / why me” interview answers — each engineered to demonstrate fit rather than gesture at it, and to read like a person rather than an obviously-generated draft.

title: Application Assistant
text:
Why I built this
Generic AI application tools write the way AI tools write. Abstract phrasing, endless em-dashes, openings that could apply to any company, sentences that stack three “intersection of X / Y / Z” clauses. The output looks polished and reads as obviously generated — exactly the wrong signal for senior roles.
The problem isn’t the writing step. It’s the thinking step. Most tools jump straight from “JD + resume” to “write,” which forces the model to invent fit on the fly. The result gestures at fit instead of proving it.
What started as a cover-letter tool grew into the whole front half of an application: the cover letter, the resume that goes with it, and the interview answers that follow. The same discipline runs through all three — identify the role’s actual problems, match them to real evidence, decide a central story, then write and strip everything that doesn’t serve it.

title: Application Assistant
text:
What I built
A single Flask app with a header mode toggle across three workflows:

✉ Cover Letter

Accepts a JD (paste or URL) and a resume upload (PDF via pdfplumber, DOCX via python-docx).
Calls Claude with a structured system prompt that forces silent pre-writing analysis — identify the role’s 2–3 biggest business problems, pick the matching resume evidence, decide a one-sentence central story — then writes.
Returns a standard business-letter cover letter under explicit anti-cliché constraints: name the company in the opening, no “I am excited to apply,” at most one em-dash in the whole letter, a hard blocklist of phrases like “sits at the intersection,” “at scale,” “growth enablement.”
Has a financial-services / credit-risk variant that frames technical work as evidence of business judgment, not as the main story.
Per-paragraph refine: re-run any single paragraph without regenerating the whole letter.



📄 Resume Tailor

Classifies the role from the JD (PM / AI-ML PM / Fintech PM / Data Science / Strategy-Ops / Hybrid).
Selects the strongest, non-overlapping bullets from three baked-in master resumes (PM, Fintech/DS-modeling, Strategy-Ops).
Rewrites the selected bullets for clarity and JD alignment with a strict no-fabrication rule.
Renders the result into a DOCX template that preserves the original formatting — swapping the summary paragraph and the fixed company bullet groups in place — and downloads a one-page file named AvaShen_[Company]_[Role]_[Date].docx.
Chat-refine loop for iterating on the tailored resume.



💬 Why Questions

Generates grounded answers to the questions that decide interviews: why this company, why this role, why me, and “what product are you most proud of building?”
Uses web search to pull real, current company facts before answering — no flattery, no invented detail.
Returns each answer in four registers (interview / recruiter / written / sharper), plus company research, memorizable talking points, an anti-generic audit of specificity and tone, and coaching notes on what to personalize or confirm.
Own refine loop that keeps facts grounded in existing sources and preserves an authentic voice rather than inflating the story.

Supporting pieces: voice dictation (OpenAI transcription) so logging notes has zero friction, and a regenerable portfolio-of-products reference the model draws on. Deploys to Render via Dockerfile + render.yaml.

title: Application Assistant
text:
How it works
The engineering lives in the prompts and the structure around them:

Analysis before generation. Every mode forces explicit, silent identification of the role’s real problems and the candidate’s strongest matching evidence before a single sentence is written. This changes the output more than any post-hoc editing prompt.
Anti-cliché rules are enumerated, not vague. “Avoid clichés” does nothing; the model is trained to write them. A named blocklist plus a one-em-dash hard limit does.
No fabrication, ever. Resume Tailor only rewrites existing evidence; Why Questions only states company facts it can ground in a real source. Authenticity is a hard constraint, not a style note.
Format-preserving DOCX rendering. Rather than generating a document from scratch, the resume renderer edits a template in place — swapping specific paragraphs and bullet groups — so the output keeps professional formatting and stays one page.
Structured outputs and refine loops. Each mode returns structured content and supports targeted refinement (a single paragraph, a single answer) without regenerating everything.

title: Application Assistant
text:
My role
Sole builder. The Flask, parsing, and DOCX layers were straightforward; the prompts and the analytical scaffolding were the real work — tuning each constraint, testing across JD types (consulting, fintech, risk, generic SaaS), and removing the specific failure modes I kept seeing. Built with Claude Code and deployed to Render with Docker.

title: Application Assistant
text:
What I learned

Quality is upstream of generation. Forcing explicit business-problem identification before writing moves the output more than any amount of editing afterward. Move the work upstream.
Anti-cliché rules have to be specific. Block phrases by name and cap the em-dashes. General instructions don’t survive contact with a model trained to write the clichés.
The most valuable feature is the silent pre-analysis. Users never see it, but it’s why the output reads like a person wrote it.
One workflow, three artifacts. Cover letter, resume, and interview answers are the same fit problem expressed three ways. Building them in one tool — sharing the analysis discipline and the candidate’s evidence — produces more coherent applications than three disconnected generators.
Authenticity beats polish for senior roles. The win wasn’t prettier text; it was output specific and grounded enough that a hiring manager couldn’t tell it was AI-assisted.

title: Startup Thesis Screener Pipeline
text:
Who it’s for
Senior operators running their own thesis-driven pipelines who need to:

Evaluate hundreds of companies at depth, not just respond to recruiter inbound or VC noise
Apply consistent scoring (problem quality, founder-market fit, AI/data leverage, defensibility) across a wide surface
Pull visa-sponsorship evidence from primary sources (MyVisaJobs, h1bgrader, USCIS) — not infer from cap tables
Refresh the universe monthly with a delta report rather than rerun the whole thing

title: Startup Thesis Screener Pipeline
text:
Architecture
flowchart TB
    A1[Discovery Agent 1<br/>NYC AI/data] --> B[Candidate files]
    A2[Discovery Agent 2<br/>Remote-friendly US] --> B
    A3[Discovery Agent 3<br/>Recent YC batches] --> B
    A4[Discovery Agent 4<br/>Tier-1 VC portfolios] --> B
    A5[Discovery Agent 5<br/>Stealth + wildcards] --> B
    A6[Discovery Agent 6<br/>Vertical sweeps] --> B
    B --> C[5 parallel scoring agents<br/>12-dimension rubric]
    C --> D[Python dedup + sort]
    D --> E[Top 50 shortlist]
    E --> F[4 parallel deep-research agents<br/>top 20 only]
    F --> G[2 visa-verification agents<br/>MyVisaJobs + h1bgrader + LCAs]
    G --> H[Final report + CSVs]

title: Startup Thesis Screener Pipeline
text:
Key design choices

Parallel agents over monolithic prompts. Each discovery agent owns one vertical or source, so eight ran in parallel instead of one slow sequential pass. Output landed in disk-persisted files — context compaction couldn’t lose hours of work.
Disk persistence between phases. Every agent wrote a Markdown or CSV file rather than returning content in chat. In a 2+ hour pipeline, this is non-negotiable.
Inline-return fallback for Write permission denials. When five of eight agents hit Write permission errors on the first run, they returned content inline as their final message. The parent agent persisted it. The pipeline survived the failure mode.
Cross-batch dedup in Python, not in agents. LLMs hallucinate “same company” matches. I deduped by normalized company name in a Python script — cheap, exact, debuggable.
Visa verification as a separate phase, not embedded. The first scoring pass inferred visa feasibility from cap table size, headcount, and HQ. The verification pass pulled live LCA records. The two passes disagreed on four of ten top picks — and the verified data produced material downgrades for several “obvious” candidates.

title: Startup Thesis Screener Pipeline
text:
Key result

Universe surveyed: 653 unique AI/data startups at seed–Series B across 14 verticals
Time investment: ~3 hours of agent runtime + ~2 hours of analyst review
Output: top-20 deep-dive case studies, top-10 with verified visa evidence, monthly-refresh template
Surprising signal: the strongest predictor of long-term visa pathway is PERM completion rate, not LCA volume. Several well-funded sponsors had 10+ LCAs but zero completed PERMs — meaning their sponsored hires consistently left before the green card finished. This shifted the recommended action plan for the top three candidates.

title: Startup Thesis Screener Pipeline
section: What I’d build differently next time
text:
What I’d build differently next time

Run discovery and scoring in the same agent pass. Separating them across two phases doubled the LLM cost and added coordination overhead with no real quality gain.
Version-control the scoring rubric separately from agent prompts. I mixed them; when I changed the rubric mid-run, I had to re-dispatch agents instead of just re-scoring existing rows.
Pre-build a legal-entity-name mapping. Several visa lookups failed because the legal entity (e.g., “Cascading AI Inc” for Casca, “Eminent INC dba Revolve Clothing” for Revolve) differs from the brand. A pre-mapping step would have saved an hour and avoided two false-negative misses.

title: Daily News Aggregator with WhatsApp Push
text:
One-line summary
A daily content pipeline that pulls articles from 12 curated tech and investment sources, filters out clickbait (~36% drop rate), deduplicates near-identical stories across publishers, summarizes the top-scoring items with Claude, and pushes the digest to WhatsApp every morning. Cuts daily news reading from ~105 minutes to ~35 minutes.

title: Daily News Aggregator with WhatsApp Push
text:
Why I built this
Tech and investment news degraded sharply through 2024–25. Three problems:

The same press release shows up across four sites. Reading “Nvidia announces DGX Spark” on Ars Technica, then The Verge, then TechCrunch, then Hacker News is the modal news-browsing experience now. Most of the time is spent recognizing duplicates, not extracting signal.
Content-farm noise expanded faster than signal. Even quality publishers are running AI-generated rewrites and SEO bait. Browsing TechCrunch homepage for thirty minutes returns five real stories.
AI summarization tools work downstream of the problem. They summarize after the noise has already filled my reading queue. The leverage point is upstream: better source curation, better deduplication, then AI for signal extraction — not a chatbot that explains the noise more concisely.

I wanted a pipeline that did the upstream work — curate sources, dedupe across publishers, AI-summarize survivors, deliver to a medium I’d actually see (WhatsApp, not another email folder I never open).

title: Daily News Aggregator with WhatsApp Push
text:
What I built
A daily content pipeline (daily_digest.py) that:

Pulls from 12 curated sources — Ars Technica, Bloomberg Markets, Hacker News, The Verge, Wired, MIT Technology Review, MarketWatch, TechCrunch, plus others — configured in config/sources.yaml
Filters clickbait and low-quality content — title heuristics + content checks; ~36% drop rate in production
Deduplicates near-identical stories across publishers — clusters by headline + first-paragraph similarity, keeps the most credible publisher in each cluster
Summarizes top-scoring articles with Claude — 2-3 sentence summary + 3-5 bullet points + relevance score (75–85/100 for AI-summarized items, 50/100 baseline for headline-only items)
Splits into Tech vs Investment categories for scan-ability
Pushes the digest to WhatsApp via Twilio — formatted text message delivered to my phone every morning
Runs via cron so it just shows up; I don’t have to remember to launch it

title: Daily News Aggregator with WhatsApp Push
text:
How it works

Source ingestion: RSS feeds for sources that publish them, light HTML scraping for the ones that don’t, all configured per-source in YAML
Filtering: title/content heuristics catch the obvious clickbait; per-source rate limits prevent over-fetching
Deduplication: cluster articles by normalized headline + first-200-token similarity; pick the highest-quality publisher in each cluster
Scoring: a relevance score is computed from source quality, topic match (tech vs investment), and recency
AI summarization: top N articles get Claude calls for structured summaries
WhatsApp delivery via Twilio: this was the highest-friction part — the 24-hour WhatsApp Business messaging window is a real product constraint (multiple helper scripts in the repo handle account-state verification, message-window checks, opt-in flow)

title: Daily News Aggregator with WhatsApp Push
text:
My role
Sole builder. Picked the source list and iterated on it (the source list is the product more than the summarization is). Wrote the dedup + scoring logic, the Claude summarization prompts, the Twilio integration with all the WhatsApp window handling. Set up the cron job so the digest just lands every morning.

title: Daily News Aggregator with WhatsApp Push
section: Output: from a real production run
text:
Output: from a real production run


Articles fetched: 33 from 12 sources
Filtered out (clickbait / low quality): 12 (36% noise drop)
Duplicates removed across sources: 11
Articles delivered to digest: 21 (8 AI-summarized + 13 with title/URL/score)
Active sources surfaced: 8 (out of 12 configured)
Average relevance (AI-summarized): 75–85/100
Operating cost: ~$1.50/month at current volume
Daily reading time: ~105 min before → ~35 min after (≈70 min/day saved)


Each AI-enhanced article in the digest includes:

Concise 2-3 sentence summary
3-5 bullet-pointed key facts
Automatic topic detection
Relevance score (typically 75-85/100)
Source and publish date
Direct link to full article

title: Daily News Aggregator with WhatsApp Push
text:
What I learned

Curation is upstream of summarization. The first version of this pipeline focused on better summaries. The second focused on better source picking and deduplication. The second was dramatically more useful — same summarization quality, much less noise to summarize.
The delivery medium matters more than the content quality. A great digest in an email folder I never open is worth less than a decent digest in a WhatsApp thread I check 50 times a day. Match the artifact to where the decision actually happens.
WhatsApp’s 24-hour Business messaging window is a real product constraint. Handling it gracefully (verify account state, opt-in flow, fallback paths, multiple helper checks) took more code than the summarization pipeline. Twilio’s docs are accurate but the failure modes are subtle.
Cost-per-decision is the right metric for personal AI. $1.50/month for ~35 hours/month of attention saved is a 2,000× return at any reasonable hourly rate. Most personal-AI tools fail the cost-per-decision test; this one passes by a wide margin.

title: SQL Case Practice Agent
text:
One-line summary
A Streamlit-based interview-prep system that generates realistic SQL scenarios with intentional edge cases (NULLs, duplicates, orphaned foreign keys, same-second timestamps), evaluates my queries with an LLM against the scenario’s actual intent, and tracks my progress across sessions in a local SQLite database.

title: SQL Case Practice Agent
text:
Why I built this
Conventional SQL interview prep fails in two specific ways.
The scenarios are too clean. LeetCode-style SQL problems and ad-hoc “ChatGPT, make me a SQL question” prompts both produce data without the dirt that real interviews test for — NULL handling, duplicate rows, orphaned foreign keys, ties on timestamps, edge cases on window functions. The questions you actually get in senior data interviews are about catching those edge cases, not about syntax.
There’s no progress signal. A practice tool that doesn’t track which patterns you’ve struggled with, what you’ve already seen, and what you keep missing isn’t a practice tool — it’s a problem generator. Real practice requires a feedback loop.
I wanted a tool that surfaced realistic interview scenarios with intentional edge cases, evaluated my queries against the scenario’s underlying intent (not just the SQL correctness), and remembered what I’d worked on so I could see my own gaps.

title: SQL Case Practice Agent
text:
What I built
A Streamlit web app that:

Generates four interview-relevant test tables — users, transactions, logins, subscriptions — populated with deliberately seeded edge cases:

NULL values in user status
Duplicate transaction rows (same txn_id, same timestamp)
Orphaned user_ids in the transactions table (FK violations against the users table)
Same-second login timestamps for the same user (window-function trap)
Varying subscription plan types and overlapping date ranges

Runs my queries against in-memory DuckDB — same ANSI-SQL semantics as Postgres-class engines, but zero setup overhead
Evaluates each query with OpenAI — does my query handle the NULLs correctly? Did I dedupe the duplicate transactions? Did I account for orphaned FKs? The LLM evaluates against the scenario’s intent, not just whether the SQL ran
Tracks progress in SQLite (progress.db) — every attempt is stored with timestamp, scenario type, query text, and pass/fail, so I can see which edge cases I keep missing

title: SQL Case Practice Agent
text:
How it works

Streamlit handles the UI and session state — text editor for the SQL, run-button, results display, evaluation panel
DuckDB runs the query against the test tables in-process. Fast, ANSI-SQL compliant, no installation
OpenAI API receives the scenario description, the seeded data, and my query, then evaluates: which edge cases did I catch, which did I miss, and what would the interview-quality answer look like
SQLite (progress.db) persists attempts across sessions — schema covers attempt timestamp, scenario tag, query text, outcome
@st.cache_data on the data generators keeps the test tables stable across re-runs in the same session

The scenarios cover the patterns I kept missing in actual interviews — that’s how I picked them. The edge cases aren’t random; they’re encoded versions of the questions I got wrong.

title: SQL Case Practice Agent
text:
My role
Sole builder. Designed the scenario taxonomy (what categories of edge cases matter for senior data interviews), wrote the test-data generator with the trap conditions, wrote the evaluation prompts that make the LLM grade against scenario intent rather than just SQL correctness, wired the persistence layer, and iterated on the prompts based on what kept slipping through.

title: SQL Case Practice Agent
text:
What I learned

The hard part of SQL interview prep isn’t writing queries — it’s recognizing the trap the interviewer is testing for. A practice tool that surfaces those traps systematically is more useful than another 200 LeetCode problems.
DuckDB is the right execution engine for a local practice tool. Same semantics as real warehouses, zero setup, instant feedback. Spinning up real Postgres for a practice loop is overkill.
The evaluation prompt is the differentiator vs. a static problem set. Anyone can generate questions; what makes this tool useful is the LLM reading what edge case the scenario tested and telling me whether my query caught it.
Progress tracking matters more than scenario variety. I get a lot more value from re-attempting the cases I’ve missed than from generating new ones.

title: Personal Networking Agent
text: Type: Product · Domain: Networking / career relationship management Stack: Next.js 15 · React 19 · TypeScript · Tailwind v4 · SQLite · Prisma · Anthropic Claude API (Opus 4.7 + Sonnet 4.6) · Google Calendar API · Web Speech API Status: Running locally on my Mac via launchd · Role: Sole builder

title: Personal Networking Agent
text:
One-line summary
A personal CRM for managing alumni, recruiters, hiring managers, founders, and warm intros across a long career — built to help me think about timing, fit, and next steps, not to send messages on my behalf.

title: Personal Networking Agent
text:
Why I built this
Networking tools mostly come in two shapes: automation bots that blast templated messages at scale, or enterprise CRMs designed for sales pipelines. Neither is what an individual professional actually needs.
The work of networking isn’t writing more messages. It’s remembering who you met, what you talked about, how warm the relationship is, what you owe them and they owe you, and — most importantly — when to follow up so you don’t seem pushy or, equally bad, forgotten. Most of that is judgment, not throughput. The bottleneck is memory and timing, not message volume.
I wanted a tool that:

intakes contacts in plain English (voice or text) — so the friction of logging a conversation is zero
holds a structured record of every interaction over time, not just a snapshot
recommends a next-best-action that’s a concrete sentence, not a vague “follow up”
decides when to follow up using both deterministic rules and contextual judgment
writes follow-up reminders to my personal Google Calendar so the prompt to act shows up where I already live
never, ever sends a message on my behalf

The hard rule is the last one. Auto-sent networking outreach feels exactly like what it is, and it burns the relationship the moment the recipient suspects it’s not really you. The judgment of whether and what to send has to stay with me.

title: Personal Networking Agent
text:
What I built
A Next.js application I run on my own Mac. Single user, no auth, fully local data.

Quick Add — type or dictate a free-form description of a contact (“I met a Columbia alum at a fintech event, she works at Citi in first-party fraud analytics, connected on LinkedIn but no reply, remind me in 7 days”). A Claude Sonnet 4.6 call with tool-use returns a fully structured contact record with ~25 fields, which I review and edit before saving.
Log new interaction — on any existing contact, I can dictate “had a 20-min call today, she’s open to introing me to her manager,” and the system parses it into a timeline entry, replaces the contact’s current status, regenerates the recommended action, and patches the calendar event in place.
Next best action engine — a deterministic rules engine (e.g. “active reply thread → 5 days,” “LinkedIn nudge no reply → 7-day nudge then 21-day, then archive at 45”) feeds a Claude Opus 4.7 call that returns both a one-sentence recommendation and a follow-up day count, with explicit guidance to lean longer when the default would feel pushy.
Google Calendar reminders — each contact gets one event on their next follow-up date. Edit the date in the app and the event moves on Calendar. Clear the date and the event is deleted. Log a new interaction and the description updates with the latest context.
Coach — a chat interface that reads the full snapshot of every active contact and answers questions like “who should I contact this week,” “draft a follow-up for Jane,” “who has accepted my LinkedIn but not replied.” Voice in, optional voice out. Read-only — can’t modify data, can’t send anything.
Bulk delete and timeline editing — checkboxes to clean up the contact list, per-row delete on the interaction timeline, manual date and action override on any contact’s recommendation card.

title: Personal Networking Agent
text:
How it works
A few choices that shaped the design:

Contact as snapshot, interactions as timeline. The contact record holds the current state (latest status, who they are, what’s next). A separate interactions table holds the append-only history of every touchpoint. The contact’s “last contact summary” is always the newest interaction; the full history is preserved underneath. Claude sees both when generating recommendations.
Cadence rules as prior, Claude as judgment layer. A small rules engine in lib/cadence.ts produces a default day count from string patterns in the contact’s status. Claude receives that default as a prior — not a ceiling — and is explicitly told to override longer when the default would feel pushy, shorter when there’s an offer or question cooling on the table. This gave a meaningful quality bump over rules-only output, especially for the “they said let’s reconnect next month” case that string-matching can’t catch.
No auth, no cloud, no exposure. The app is single-user and lives on my Mac. SQLite holds the data. A macOS LaunchAgent runs the production build on login and restarts it on crash. No public URL. No login screen needed, because the device itself is the access boundary.
Prompt caching everywhere it matters. The intake parsing system prompt, the cadence rules, and the coach’s instructions are all marked cache_control: ephemeral. The first call writes the cache; every subsequent call within the 5-min window reads it at ~10% the cost. For the coach in particular — which ships a snapshot of every active contact in every turn — this kept per-question cost in the single-digit cents range even with adaptive thinking on.
Tool use for structured extraction, messages.create for everything else. Anywhere the model needs to return strict structured output (intake parsing, NBA recommendation with day count), the call uses tool use with a Zod-validated schema and tool_choice forced to the tool name. Anywhere it’s open-ended (coach replies, message drafts), it’s plain text generation.
Voice as a first-class input, not an add-on. The browser’s built-in webkitSpeechRecognition handles dictation everywhere: intake, log interaction, coach. The coach has an “auto-send after voice” toggle so you can push to talk, release, and have it fire — no extra click. Optional speechSynthesis for replies, so it can be a hands-free conversation.

title: Personal Networking Agent
text:
My role
Sole builder. Built and shipped in roughly a day and a half across architecture, scaffolding, the schema and API surface, the cadence engine, the OAuth flow for Calendar, the voice integration, and the production deployment via launchd. Used Claude Code as the development environment.

title: Personal Networking Agent
text:
What I learned

The judgment layer is more valuable than the automation layer. I started by building rules for cadence, then put Claude on top of them. The rules alone produced recommendations that felt mechanical (“3 days for active threads”) and were often wrong for the specific contact. Adding Claude as the override layer — with explicit guidance about when to lean longer — closed most of that gap without sacrificing the determinism of the defaults. The tool is most useful when it has opinions, not when it follows a flowchart.
Auto-send is a feature ceiling, not a floor. It’s the obvious next thing to build, and it’s the thing that would make the product worth less, not more. The whole point is that the user remains the sender. Anything that looks like a templated outreach immediately defeats the purpose of personal networking. The product is more useful precisely because it doesn’t do the most automatable thing.
Tool use is the right shape for structured intake. Versus prompt-engineered JSON output, forced tool_choice with a Zod-validated schema gave me predictable extraction with very few retries. The intake parser handles partial information cleanly — every field nullable — which matches how people actually describe contacts (rarely with a full bio in one go).
Calendar is a better persistence layer than the app itself for the “act now” moment. I don’t want to open the networking tool to check who to reach out to today. I want to see “Follow up: Jane Doe — Citi” on my calendar where I’m already looking. Treating Google Calendar as the source-of-truth for when to act, and the app as the source-of-truth for who/why/what, kept both surfaces honest about their role.
Personal-use software has different deploy semantics than product software. This doesn’t need to be on Vercel. It doesn’t need real auth. It doesn’t need a Postgres tier. Running it on my own Mac with launchd auto-start gives me persistent local access, zero ongoing cost, and an attack surface of exactly one device. The right deploy for a single-user tool is the boring one.

title: H-1B / PERM Sponsor Search — Structured Employer Prioritization
text: Type: Analysis (decision-support pipeline) · Domain: US employment-based immigration / employer hiring data Sources: H1BGrader · MyVisaJobs · H1BData.info · USCIS H-1B Employer Data Hub · ICE SEVIS top-200 STEM-OPT employers · DOL OFLC public disclosures Status: Live working analysis · Role: Analyst

title: H-1B / PERM Sponsor Search — Structured Employer Prioritization
text:
Core question
For a candidate on F-1 STEM OPT looking to bridge to H-1B and then PERM at a senior IC level, the standard “list of sponsors” is misleading. Most “top 100 H-1B employers” lists are dominated by IT staffing firms running cap-exempt transfers — useless for someone targeting product / risk / analytics / strategy roles at companies that actually run senior IC ladders.
The real question:

Out of all US employers with public visa-sponsorship evidence, which 100 actually sponsor senior IC and director-level hires through the H-1B cap lottery AND have followed through with PERM at scale — at companies whose roles match a financial services, decision systems, or AI-product profile?

title: H-1B / PERM Sponsor Search — Structured Employer Prioritization
text:
Why this matters
A bad sponsorship match wastes a year of cap-lottery cycles and risks a PERM that never completes. The downstream consequence of getting this wrong is 6–7 years of uncertainty.
The data exists publicly — DOL OFLC LCA disclosures, USCIS H-1B Employer Data Hub, ICE SEVIS STEM-OPT top-200, plus MyVisaJobs / H1BGrader / H1BData.info aggregations — but it’s fragmented across 5+ sources with different fiscal-year cuts, different legal-entity-name conventions, and very different reliability levels. Standard “top sponsor” rankings combine signal that shouldn’t be combined.
I built a structured pipeline to turn the fragmented data into a decision-ready shortlist.

title: H-1B / PERM Sponsor Search — Structured Employer Prioritization
text:
Method

Generated a candidate company universe from US large- and mid-cap firms across financial services, data infrastructure, fintech, healthcare/biopharma data, enterprise SaaS, decision intelligence, and tech-consulting — the sectors with role surfaces matching a senior FS / analytics / AI-product profile.
Pulled LCA filing counts and PERM filings per company from H1BGrader, MyVisaJobs, and H1BData.info — cross-referenced across all three to catch legal-entity-name variants (e.g., “Capital One Services LLC” vs. “Capital One Financial Corp,” “Bloomberg LP” vs. subsidiaries).
Verified E-Verify enrollment using the ICE SEVIS top-200 STEM-OPT employer list plus direct careers-page checks where possible. E-Verify is a hard requirement for STEM OPT extension — companies that aren’t enrolled are non-starters regardless of how many H-1Bs they file.
Categorized H-1B cap vs. transfer behavior. Excluded staffing firms and bodyshops outright. Flagged companies whose pattern looked like cap-exempt transfers (Verisk pattern: 0 LCAs FY2025) or unusual subsidiary structures (Fidelity pattern: 0 LCAs but 303 USCIS petitions — likely cap-exempt or filing under a different legal entity).
Scored each company on five dimensions:

STEM OPT support (E-Verify enrollment evidence)
H-1B cap-lottery sponsorship volume (specifically new cap filings, not transfers)
PERM completion evidence (the green-card follow-through signal, not just initial filings)
Role-type fit (does the company actually hire senior FS / analytics / AI-product ICs?)
Source confidence (how recent, how well-cross-referenced)

Tagged each company with a strategy bucket: Immigration Safe / Bridge Role / Fit High but Sponsorship Unclear / Caution / Future Upgrade / Exclude.

title: H-1B / PERM Sponsor Search — Structured Employer Prioritization
text:
Key findings
From the 100-company analysis:








Strategy tag
Count
Description




Immigration Safe
19
High-volume sponsor + verified E-Verify + PERM track record + strong role-fit. Examples: Databricks, Snowflake, Stripe, DoorDash, Airbnb, Capital One, Two Sigma, BlackRock, Citadel Securities, S&P Global, Mastercard, Affirm.


Bridge Role
55
Sponsorship pattern is solid; role surface is narrower for senior FS/analytics IC. The right target for a 1–2 year cap-lottery bridge while building toward Immigration Safe + strong role-fit options.


Fit High / Sponsorship Unclear
7
Smaller companies (Hightouch, Monte Carlo, Harness) with strong role-fit but thin sponsorship signal — needs direct verification before relying on.


Caution
3
Verisk (0 LCAs FY2025 — significant red flag), Fidelity (unusual 0-LCA / 303-petition pattern — flagged for entity-mapping).


Excluded
(separate list)
Lemonade (explicit “we are unable to sponsor”), Compass (0 FY2026 LCAs), all IT staffing firms.



The highest-confidence insights:

LCA volume is a misleading metric on its own. Several large-volume sponsors are running transfers, not new cap. The signal that matters for a STEM-OPT candidate is new cap-lottery filing volume specifically. Verisk’s drop to 0 LCAs FY2025 was the clearest red flag in the dataset, even though they’d historically been a strong sponsor.
PERM completion rate, not LCA count, predicts the green-card outcome. Some companies file many H-1Bs but rarely follow through with PERM at scale — sponsored employees consistently leave before the green card completes. This shifts the recommended target list materially: the right metric is “% of H-1B cohort that still works there at PERM completion,” not “how many H-1Bs filed last year.”
The Bridge Role category is the most useful product of the analysis. 55 companies have sponsorship infrastructure but a role surface that isn’t natively senior-FS-IC. They’re the right targets for a cap-lottery bridge during the first 1–2 years.
A second pass expanded the universe to mid-sized and smaller sponsors where the cap-lottery odds are structurally better (smaller applicant pool per company). This surfaced several FS / AI startups that don’t appear on standard “top sponsor” lists but have real sponsorship behavior.

title: H-1B / PERM Sponsor Search — Structured Employer Prioritization
text:
Recommendation
Don’t optimize for the top of the H-1B sponsor leaderboard. Optimize for the intersection of:

Demonstrated PERM follow-through (not just LCA filing count)
Role surface that matches the candidate’s senior-IC profile (not just any open role)
E-Verify confirmation (hard prerequisite for STEM-OPT extension)

The Immigration Safe + strong-role-fit overlap is small but non-zero — those are the high-value targets for direct application. The Bridge Role list is where most candidates should actually apply during the first cap-lottery cycle to maximize lottery odds while role-skill compounds in parallel.

title: H-1B / PERM Sponsor Search — Structured Employer Prioritization
text:
What I’d investigate next

PERM cohort outcomes — of the H-1Bs each top target sponsored 3–5 years ago, what percentage were still at the company at PERM completion vs. departed? This is the actual signal that matters, and it’s reconstructible from cross-year LCA data with entity-mapping.
Subsidiary-level entity mapping — large parent companies file under different legal entities (Fidelity pattern is the obvious case). Better entity mapping would close the false-negative gap on several large sponsors.
Cap-exempt employers as a separate analysis — research universities, qualifying non-profits, and government contractors have entirely different sponsorship dynamics not captured in the standard cap-lottery framing. Worth a separate scan.

title: H-1B / PERM Sponsor Search — Structured Employer Prioritization
text:
Deliverables

100-company shortlist CSV with full scoring, source citations, strategy tags
Summary memo with category breakdowns, data-quality notes, and the specific entity-mapping flags that affect interpretation
Expanded second-pass dataset (~mid/small sponsor targets) with additional FS / AI-startup coverage where the standard “top sponsor” lists miss

All available on request. Refreshed semi-monthly as new fiscal-year filings post to DOL OFLC.

title: AI Startup Landscape — 653 Companies, May 2026
text:
The AI startup landscape in May 2026 contained roughly 5,000–10,000 companies globally at seed–Series B claiming some AI/data wedge. Standard job-search advice — “apply broadly, see what sticks” — doesn’t survive a universe where most companies are too early to sponsor a visa, too engineering-only to need a senior data operator, or too AI-veneer to last 24 months.
The question I needed an answer to: out of the addressable universe of vertical-AI / data-infrastructure / forward-deployed-AI startups, which ~10 are worth a serious application and interview cycle?

Standard job-search advice — “apply broadly, see what sticks” — doesn’t survive a universe where most companies are too early to sponsor a visa, too engineering-only to need a senior data operator, or too AI-veneer to last 24 months.
The question I needed an answer to: out of the addressable universe of vertical-AI / data-infrastructure / forward-deployed-AI startups, which ~10 are worth a serious application and interview cycle?

title: AI Startup Landscape — 653 Companies, May 2026
text:
What I did
Built and ran a multi-agent screening pipeline (see Startup Screener Pipeline) across the AI/data startup universe at seed-Series B. The pipeline:

Surveyed 653 unique companies across 14 verticals (insurance, healthcare, fintech back-office, legal, PropTech, climate, HR, GTM, data infra, AI evals, stealth, wildcards)
Scored each on 12 dimensions weighted toward problem quality, defensibility, founder-market fit, immigration feasibility, and fit for a senior data/AI/operator profile
Deep-researched the top 20 with 18-section case studies
Verified visa evidence for the top 10 via primary-source LCA databases
Identified 3 actionable tiers: apply directly (5), find warm intro (3), monitor (2)

Sources: AlleyWatch funding announcements, TechCrunch, BusinessWire, Crunchbase, YC company directory, Tier-1 VC portfolio pages, Wellfound, niche industry press (Modern Healthcare, Insurance Journal, FinTech Futures, LegalTech News), MyVisaJobs, h1bgrader, h1bdata, USCIS E-Verify employer search, Glassdoor, LinkedIn.

title: AI Startup Landscape — 653 Companies, May 2026
text:
Key findings

1. The senior-IC visible job-title taxonomy at AI startups is converging on “Forward-Deployed Engineer,” “AI Strategist,” and “Deployed Intelligence” — not “Data Scientist”
At most vertical-AI startups (Palantir-DNA companies especially), the senior-IC role for someone with a 10-year analytics background is not titled “Data Scientist.” That title often gets junior-coded or sits behind a PhD bar. The senior seats that map cleanly to an FS-analytics / decision-science profile carry titles like Forward Deployed Engineer, AI Strategist, Deployed Intelligence Strategist, or Solutions Architect.
Implication: Searching for “Senior Data Scientist” openings will systematically miss the best-fit seats.


2. PERM completion rate matters more than LCA volume
The conventional metric for “does this company sponsor visas?” is LCA filing count. I found this metric is misleading. Several companies in the verified top 10 had 10+ LCAs filed but 0 completed PERM applications — meaning sponsored employees consistently left before the green card process completed. One mature retailer outside the AI cohort had filed 11 PERM applications and only 1 was ever certified (the rest expired).
Implication: For a 6-7 year H-1B-to-PERM horizon, you want to verify PERM completion rate, not just LCA volume. Ask in the first recruiter call: “Has anyone in your data/analytics team completed PERM here?”


3. Insurance and healthcare AI verticals systematically over-index for senior-IC fit
Of the top 20 companies by priority, 8 operated in regulated insurance or healthcare workflow domains (claims, underwriting, prior auth, denial management, RCM). These domains punish AI-veneer plays — the customers (carriers, hospitals, RCM teams) demand evidence and audit trails. They reward decision-science discipline and risk-modeling skill that transfers cleanly from financial services.
Implication: If you have FS analytics background, vertical-AI startups in insurance/healthcare/compliance are the cleanest skill transfer — better than horizontal AI infrastructure or pure dev tooling.


4. Geography and visa cluster: NYC + Series A+ + culturally-international founder is the strongest sponsorship-feasibility combination
Among the verified visa sponsors in the screen, the modal profile was: NYC-headquartered (or with a confirmed NYC office), Series A or later, and a founding team that included at least one international-origin operator. This combination shows up disproportionately in the visa-confirmed top tier.
Implication: If visa is a constraint, focus the search on NYC + Series A+ + international-co-founder companies first. SF-only seed-stage is a worse bet on visa axis even when the company is otherwise excellent.


5. “Cursor for X” / “AI agent marketplace” plays were the most consistently downrated category
In the YC W26 batch and recent seed announcements, ~10% of companies were “Cursor for [vertical]” or horizontal AI-agent marketplaces. The screen systematically downrated these:

Cursor-for-X plays have a 12-24 month window before Microsoft Copilot ships the equivalent in the underlying surface
Horizontal agent marketplaces have unclear buyer (who pays?), unclear trust mechanism (who verifies agent quality?), and unclear repeat-usage economics
A higher percentage of these companies (vs. vertical-AI peers) scored above 4 on the Hype/BS-Risk dimension

Implication: Treat these categories with extra skepticism. They generate fundraising press but the unit economics often don’t survive the first refresh of the underlying foundation model.

title: AI Startup Landscape — 653 Companies, May 2026
text:
Recommendation
For an immigrant senior data IC targeting AI/data startups in 2026:

Filter aggressively on visa-confirmed companies. Don’t trust inferred-from-cap-table signals. Pull primary-source LCA + PERM data before investing interview cycles.
Apply to NYC + Series A+ + culturally-international-founder targets first. This profile has the best visa odds.
Target vertical-AI in regulated industries. Insurance, healthcare, compliance, RegTech, and finance back-office reward the same skills your FS analytics background built.
Target Forward-Deployed Engineer / AI Strategist / Solutions Architect titles, not Data Scientist. The senior-IC compensation tier hides under these names.
Negotiate PERM commitment in writing at offer stage. Companies with LCA history but no PERM precedent need an explicit commitment.

title: AI Startup Landscape — 653 Companies, May 2026
text:
What surprised me
The biggest surprise was the gap between inferred visa friendliness and verified visa friendliness. The initial scoring pass scored ~60% of “visa-friendly” candidates correctly when checked against MyVisaJobs / h1bgrader. The rest were corrected — usually downward — by primary-source verification. The inference signal (cap table size, headcount, NYC HQ) is correlated with but not equal to actual sponsorship willingness.
Second surprise: the founders’ national-origin background was a stronger predictor of sponsorship culture than the company’s funding stage. Two well-funded SF Series B companies with all-US-citizen founders sponsored less than a smaller Series A with a foreign-born CEO.

title: AI Startup Landscape — 653 Companies, May 2026
text:
What I’d interrogate further

PERM cohort outcomes. Of the H-1B holders sponsored 3+ years ago at top targets, how many are still at the company today vs. departed? This is the actual signal that matters.
Job-title-to-LCA mapping at scale. I’d want to systematically map every job posting to the LCA-sponsored titles by company, so I could automatically flag postings unlikely to result in a visa-sponsorable role.
Cross-vertical second-order effects. Several “horizontal AI infra” companies in my screen had FS customer overlap (Stripe, Brex, Plaid). The FS background creates a usable wedge there even when the company isn’t FS-vertical.

title: AI Startup Landscape — 653 Companies, May 2026
text:
Data & code
Underlying company data and rankings are private (commercial sensitivity around individual companies and visa inferences). The methodology and scoring framework are documented in the Startup Screener Pipeline write-up.
The pipeline can be re-run monthly using the delta-template I built. As of this analysis date (May 2026), the universe had been refreshed twice — once in the initial scan and once via targeted gap-fill across underserved verticals (Legal, PropTech, HR, Climate).
